chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Hammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he heard him saying:

"Indeed, Al-Anfal (the spoils/gains) are any land where there was no shedding of blood or where people were reconciled and gave with their own hands. And whatever is from abandoned land or the bellies of valleys, this is all from Al-Fay'. And Al-Anfal are for Allah and the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family). And whatever is for Allah, it is for the Messenger, who places it where he wills."

key_terms.أَرْضٍ خَرِبَةٍ: Abandoned land, land left without an owner
key_terms.الْأَنْفَالُ: The spoils or gains, specifically lands acquired without battle or through reconciliation
key_terms.الْفَيْءُ: The booty or gains, specifically referring to abandoned lands or property
key_terms.بُطُونِ أَوْدِيَةٍ: Bellies of valleys, referring to uncultivated or natural lands
key_terms.بِأَيْدِيهِمْ: With their own hands, indicating voluntary payment or surrender
key_terms.صُولِحُوا: They were reconciled, referring to peace treaties
key_terms.هِرَاقَةُ دَمٍ: Shedding of blood, referring to military conquest

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Anfal and Fay in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between 'Al-Anfal' (lands acquired via treaty or voluntary submission without combat) and 'Al-Fay'' (lands not tied to specific battles, such as abandoned territories). This narration underscores the Imam's role in the distribution of these resources, reflecting the Shia understanding of the Prophet's and Imams' authority over public wealth as divine trusteeship, a concept deeply rooted in the interpretation of Surah Al-Anfal and Surah Al-Hashr.
